dispute.claim_text: I bought the premium fitness program because the sales page said it included weekly one-on-one coaching. After paying, there is no coaching - only prerecorded videos. The page appears to have been changed since, and I did not save a screenshot.

evidence.text: Purchase confirmation: 'Premium Fitness Program', USD 250.00. No feature breakdown in the receipt.
Cardholder to merchant: 'The sales page said premium included weekly 1-on-1 coaching when I bought it. There is no coaching, only prerecorded videos. Please refund.'
Merchant reply: 'Coaching has never been included in this tier.' No copy of the sales page as it appeared at the time of purchase is provided.

labels.notes: Medium, genuinely gatherable. The cardholder plausibly relied on an advertised feature (weekly 1-on-1 coaching) the premium tier does not deliver - a misrepresentation of what was sold, not a quality complaint, so 13.5-r2 is consumer-supported in nature. But the critical point is a gap: the cardholder has no proof the sales page made that claim (no screenshot), and the merchant's denial (ev_003) is an assertion, not proof of the original page. Unlike a dead case, this is gatherable - the original page can often be recovered from a web archive or cache, or the marketing email that made the claim. Honest output: insufficient, with a prompt to produce the original listing; if obtained, it would flip to fight.
